Four-neighbor edges were compared within square neighborhoods at tolerances of 1, 2, and 4 pixels.
Many-to-one matches are allowed, irrespective of orientation or flanking cluster labels. This proximity measure differs from boundary-detection precision and recall.
The rate was undefined when the source set was empty and was zero when the source set was nonempty but the target set was empty.
We included the same specimens at all scales, requiring both directions to be defined for every planned pair at all three tolerances. We did not impute missing values.
Each metric was averaged over pairs per specimen, then summarized by the equally weighted mean and sample standard deviation across specimens. All 49 contributed to every metric and comparison group. Internal boundary positions were similar across repetitions, including comparisons with the first map (Table F.2 ).
Comparisons across representations had lower ARI and higher VI than those within a representation. Even at a one-pixel tolerance, their lower directed agreement rate averaged 0.879.
Agreement with the first map varied by specimen. The lowest specimen means over the eight pairs were 0.689, 0.743, and 0.810 at 1, 2, and 4 pixels, respectively.
These rates lack chance correction, and denser boundaries favor nearby matches. We therefore consider both directions and their variation across specimens. Qualitative comparison of the maps across repetitions consistently showed characteristic regions interpreted as degradation-related and distributions following latewood in softwoods.
Assignments varied more visibly in interior regions considered less affected by surface degradation or aging, except where features such as latewood were distinct.
In regions with small spectral differences, quantization of the latent representations may have produced different partitions across repetitions, changing which pixels were grouped together and thereby contributing to the lower ARI. These observations and the similarity of boundary configurations support the stability of the maps as a basis for interpreting local features in relation to surrounding distributions.
We examine the chemical meaning of each region using the material in Appendix G , relating NIR spectral features and spatial distributions to literature band assignments and specimen information (Section 6.4 ).

与第一张地图的协议因标本而异。 最低标本表示在8对以上分别是0.689,0.743和0.810,分别是1,2和4像素.
这些比率缺乏概率校正,更密集的界限有利于附近的匹配. 因此,我们考虑双向及其不同标本的差异。 对重复的地图进行定性比较,始终显示出被解释为与退化有关的特征区域,以及软木中晚木的分布。
在不太受地表退化或老化影响的内陆地区,任务差异较大,但诸如晚林等特征不同的情况除外。
在光谱差异小的区域,对潜在表示的量化可能会产生不同重复的分区,改变将哪一个像素组合在一起,从而促成较低的ARI. 这些观测结果和边界布局的相似性支持了地图的稳定性,作为解释周边分布的局部特征的基础.
我们利用附录G中的材料,将国家清单报告谱系特征和空间分布与文献波段分配和标本信息联系起来,审查每个区域的化学含义(第6.4节)。

Appendix G NIR Band Assignments and Specimen Maps G.1 NIR Band Assignments Table F.2 gives the assignments corresponding to the numbered bands in Figures and G.1 .
We used Table 2 and the accompanying text in the review by Schwanninger et al. [42] as a starting point and checked the assignments against original studies comparing wood with isolated lignin and cellulose [ 15 ] , assigning bands in cellulosic paper [ 2 ] , and examining water–polymer interactions [ 36 ] .
The assignment of band 7 to semicrystalline cellulose [ 52 ] and the description of the combination band at band 16 [ 45 ] follow the respective original studies.
At band 12, an assignment to CH 3 in the acetyl groups of xylan has also been reported [ 14 ] , leaving the specific vibrational assignment open.
At band 10, aromatic extractives may contribute alongside lignin [ 48 ] .
The table distinguishes the component assignments from the vibrational details and contributions of other components at nearby wavenumbers. Table G.1: Literature assignments for the numbered bands in Figures and G.1 . No. Wavenumber (cm -1 ) Assigned constituents Vibration Interpretation 1 8547 Lignin Second overtone of asymmetric unsaturated C–H stretching (HC=CH) Lignin-related C–H band, distinct from the aromatic C–H band at band 10. 2 8420–8370 Lignin, possible cellulose contribution Second overtone of C–H stretching A CH 3 assignment has been reported. This band is not specific to lignin. 3 8250–8160 Cellulose Second overtone of C–H stretching Includes several C–H bands. Assignments to individual CH and CH 2 groups are tentative. 4 7321–7315 Cellulose Combination of the first overtone of C–H stretching and C–H bending — 5 7003–6993 Water, amorphous polysaccharides First overtone of O–H stretching (polysaccharides) Free or weakly hydrogen-bonded O–H. Glucomannan and xylan contribute alongside cellulose. 6 6974–6954 Water, amorphous polysaccharides Combination of symmetric and asymmetric O–H stretching in water (main water contribution) and first overtone of polysaccharide O–H stretching Absorption by water and amorphous polysaccharides overlaps. Interpret together with band 5 to assess differences in the hydrogen-bonding environment. 7 6757 Cellulose (semicrystalline regions) First overtone of O–H stretching Weak hydrogen bonding in cellulose and adsorbed water have also been reported to contribute nearby. 8 6450 Cellulose (crystalline regions) First overtone of hydrogen-bonded O–H stretching Nearby assignments to intrachain hydrogen bonding and to cellulose I α \alpha overlap. 9 6281 Cellulose (crystalline regions) First overtone of strongly hydrogen-bonded O–H stretching Several intra- and interchain hydrogen bonds have been assigned in this region. 10 5980–5963 Lignin, aromatic extractives First overtone of aromatic C–H stretching CH 3 in hemicellulose acetyl groups contributes on either side, near 6003 and 5950 cm -1 . 11 5890 Lignin First overtone of C–H stretching Also observed in isolated lignin. The type of C–H group remains uncertain. 12 5865 Hemicellulose First overtone of C–H stretching Assignments to CH 2 and to CH 3 in xylan acetyl groups have both been reported. A cellulose C–H contribution has been reported nearby at 5872 cm -1 . 13 5795 Lignin First overtone of C–H stretching Also observed in isolated lignin. Hemicellulose contributes nearby at about 5800 cm -1 . 14 5776 Cellulose First overtone of C–H stretching The assignment to CH 2 is tentative. 15 5577 Cellulose, lignin First overtone of C–H stretching In addition to cellulosic paper, isolated lignin shows absorption at 5578 cm -1 . 16 5464 Cellulose (semicrystalline and crystalline regions) Combination of O–H stretching and the first overtone of C–O stretching Interpret together with O–H bands 7–9 to assess features associated with crystalline and semicrystalline regions. 17 5220–5150 Water Combination of asymmetric O–H stretching and H–O–H bending Reflects bound water in the cell wall under air-dry conditions. Hydrogen bonding with polymers affects its position and shape. 18 4392 Cellulose Combination of O–H and C–C stretching, and/or of C–H stretching and C–H bending Both combinations have been proposed, leaving the specific vibrational assignment open. The vertical lines in the figures mark literature wavenumbers associated with the troughs at which we compared changes. Wavenumber ranges encompass values reported in multiple sources.
Overlapping absorption bands and differentiation can affect the position and depth of a trough.
We therefore considered multiple bands associated with each component together, without assuming that neighboring band numbers correspond to independently resolved peaks.
We did not convert these assignments directly into component quantities or degrees of degradation.

The maps in Figure G.1 show all pixel assignments from full-dataset fitting of M11 for each of the 49 specimens.
For each specimen, we show second-derivative NIR spectra for clusters whose assigned pixels formed visually discernible regions in its map (Section 5.4 ), with any additional reference spectra labeled by source specimen.

Appendix E.2 compares the spatial maps from full-dataset fitting under the six main conditions.

Figure G.1: M11 spatial maps and second-derivative NIR spectra for all 49 specimens.
Each specimen is shown with its map and local enlargement on the left and its spectra on the right.
Map colors, color-bar numbers, and spectral line colors denote cluster IDs.
On the measured transverse surfaces, the arrows mark perimeter segments corresponding to side surfaces of the original timber member that were exposed during service.
Dotted boxes enclose the regions adjacent to those surfaces that are shown enlarged.
Spectral band numbers 1–18 correspond to Table F.2 . In the spectral plots, arrows and vertical dotted lines indicate the literature-assigned wavenumbers used for the comparisons.
Gray bands indicate wavenumber ranges reported in the literature. Regions (a)–(c) are shown enlarged.
The legend gives the specimen ID when a spectrum from another specimen is included for reference.
Triangles mark spectral values outside the displayed vertical range.
